To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the forward translocational force is generated by the contraction of an actomyosin network in a transition zone between lamellipodia of keratocytes and the cell body.

the forward translocations of cell body are driven by the actin– myosin II network in the lamella/ cell body boundary zone, and the myosin II clusters are stationary with respect to substratum, but they are transported to the boundary zone in the lamella, where they become compressed and aligned, leading to the boundary bundles.

the actin– myosin II system of fish keratocytes exhibits a complex organization in lamellipodial–cell body transition zone, and the mechanism of cell locomotion in keratocytes involves the contraction of an actomyosin network in this zone.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of cell motility.
the molecular mechanisms of cell locomotion.
the mechanism of the cell body translocation of fish keratocytes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mechanism of cell translocation is a result of a combination of the actin polymerization and myosin II contraction in the transition zone between the lamellipodium and the cell body.

the actin– myosin II system in fish epidermis keratocytes is composed of two distinct actin networks: one is the lamellipodium and another is the actin–cell body transition zone, where myosin II is concentrated and actin filaments are aligned.
the actin– myosin II system in keratocytes is not organized in a manner that would support either a sarcomere-like mechanism or polarized transport mechanism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the actin– myosin system in the lamellapodia is organized in such a way that it generates force in the direction of cell movement, but that the cell body translocation is driven by the contraction of the actin-myosin network in transition zone between the lamellipodium and the cell body.
the actin–Myosins II system is a major player in the cell locomotion and the cell body translocation of fish epidermal cells.
the actin– myosin system is organized in such a way that the actin filaments are polarized with the barbed ends pointing forward and myosin is localized in the cell body boundary.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the actin– myosin system in the transition zone is the driving force for cell body translocation and retrograde flow.
myosin II is not transported in the lamellae of the lamellae, but that it is transported in the lamella.
the mechanism of cell locomotion can be explained by the actin polymerization–driven protrusion and the contraction-driven translocation of the actin network.
